source_metadata.title: Clinical outcomes of antifungal therapy on Candida pulmonary colonisation in immunocompetent patients with invasive ventilation: a systematic review and meta-analysis

source_type_boundary.handling: The uploaded source is secondary literature. Atoms represent independently reviewable assertions reported by this systematic review/meta-analysis itself; claims from the nine underlying primary studies were not re-extracted as if directly verified from those primary sources.

extraction_limitations: The @ATOM workflow is designed for primary literature, but the uploaded article is a systematic review and meta-analysis.
The uploaded 7-page PDF references online supplementary tables and figures that were not contained in the uploaded file; supplementary-only details were not invented or imported.
The total number of individual patients across the nine included studies is not reported in the main-text PDF and was not inferred.

Antifungal drug identity, dose, route, and duration were not consistently reported in the main text, so exposure descriptors remain intentionally generic except for the inhaled and intravenous treatment-type subgroups explicitly reported in the abstract.
All atoms remain review_status=needs_review because this extraction was performed by a language model without independent human verification.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review aimed to establish the influence of antifungal therapy on pulmonary Candida colonisation in mechanically ventilated patients.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: This study aimed to use systematic review and meta-analysis to establish the influence of antifungal therapy on pulmonary Candida colonisation of patients with mechanical ventilation (MV).

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors searched PubMed, Web of Science, Medline, Embase, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Data, and VIP Databases from inception through 25 July 2023.
The literature search had no language restrictions, and reference lists of relevant studies were evaluated to enlarge the search scope.
Two researchers independently screened titles and abstracts and reviewed potentially eligible full texts; disagreements were resolved with a third researcher.
Eligible studies were randomised trials, cohort studies, or case-control studies of adults aged at least 18 years with pulmonary Candida colonisation after invasive ventilation.

population.label: Eligible study population
inclusion_criteria: Adults aged >=18 years
Pulmonary Candida colonisation after invasive ventilation
Randomised trial, cohort, or case-control design

atoms.canonical_statement: Pulmonary Candida colonisation was defined as Candida detected in bronchoalveolar lavage, endotracheal aspirate, protected brush specimens, or any positive airway secretion specimen.

outcome.definition: Presence of Candida in bronchoalveolar lavage, endotracheal aspiration, protected brush specimens, or any positive airway secretion specimen.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review excluded case reports, pregnant or immunocompromised patients, patients treated with antifungals for reasons other than Candida colonisation, and patients with candidemia or invasive candidiasis.

population.label: Excluded study populations
exclusion_criteria: Antifungal treatment for reasons other than Candida colonisation

atoms.canonical_statement: Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane risk assessment tool for randomised controlled trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort and case-control studies; studies scoring at least six points were considered high quality and included.
ICU mortality was a primary outcome of the review.
Hospital mortality was a primary outcome of the review.
28-day mortality was a primary outcome of the review.
90-day mortality was a primary outcome of the review.
ICU length of stay was a secondary outcome of the review.
Mechanical ventilation duration was a secondary outcome of the review.
Ventilator-associated pneumonia was a secondary outcome of the review.
Dichotomous outcomes were pooled as odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals.
Continuous outcomes were pooled as standardised mean differences with 95% confidence intervals.

The meta-analysis used inverse-variance fixed-effect models when heterogeneity was not significant at p>0.1 and random-effects models when heterogeneity was significant at p<0.1; heterogeneity was quantified with I-squared.
Sensitivity analysis used leave-one-study-out exclusion to assess result stability.
Publication bias was not assessed because fewer than 10 studies were included.
The search identified 2,947 records; after removing 1,246 duplicates and excluding 1,670 irrelevant records, 31 reports were assessed for eligibility and 9 studies were included.
The nine included studies comprised seven retrospective cohort studies, one case-control study, and one randomised clinical trial.

population.label: Nine included studies: 7 retrospective cohort, 1 case-control, 1 randomised clinical trial

atoms.canonical_statement: Among the nine included studies, two were conducted in North America, five in Europe, and two in Asia.

population.label: Nine included studies: 2 North America, 5 Europe, 2 Asia

atoms.canonical_statement: All nine included studies were assessed by the review authors as high quality.
Antifungal treatment versus no antifungal treatment showed no statistically significant difference in ICU mortality (OR 1.37, 95% CI 0.84 to 2.22; 3 studies).

atoms.canonical_statement: The forest plot reported heterogeneity for ICU mortality of I-squared 42.7% (p=0.175).
The forest plot reported heterogeneity for Hospital mortality of I-squared 74.4% (p=0.002).
The forest plot reported heterogeneity for 28-day mortality of I-squared 0.0% (p=0.463).
The forest plot reported heterogeneity for 90-day mortality of I-squared 54.8% (p=0.110).
The forest plot reported heterogeneity for ICU length of stay of I-squared 92.8% (p=0.000).
The forest plot reported heterogeneity for Mechanical ventilation duration of I-squared 93.6% (p=0.000).
The forest plot reported heterogeneity for Ventilator-associated pneumonia of I-squared 85.0% (p=0.000).
In the treatment-type subgroup analysis, inhaled antifungal therapy had a pooled odds ratio of 2.32 (95% CI 0.30 to 18.09).
In the treatment-type subgroup analysis, intravenous antifungal therapy had a pooled odds ratio of 0.65 (95% CI 0.13 to 3.34).
Leave-one-study-out sensitivity analysis did not materially change the pooled result; pooled odds ratios ranged from 1.00 (95% CI 0.51 to 1.96) to 2.07 (95% CI 0.74 to 5.78).
The authors concluded that antifungal treatment did not improve clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated patients with respiratory Candida colonisation.
The authors did not recommend antifungal medication for decolonisation of mechanically ventilated patients with respiratory Candida colonisation.

The authors proposed that a prospective randomised controlled trial would be more appropriate to evaluate antifungal treatment in mechanically ventilated patients with respiratory Candida colonisation.
Most included studies were retrospective, raising concerns about external validity.
Antifungal drug style, name, dose, and administration method were incompletely reported across included studies.
The meta-analysis was limited by the small number of included studies, especially for individual outcomes such as ICU mortality.
Most included studies were cohort studies rather than randomised controlled trials.
The authors noted limited sample size and wide 95% confidence intervals, requiring further studies to verify the findings.
The study was funded by the Changsha Municipal Health Committee (No. KJ-B2023032).
The authors declared no competing interests.
Data are available upon reasonable request.
